scenes.title: dbt Tests (Generic & Singular)
scenes.narration: This lesson explains how dbt tests catch data quality problems automatically, covering both reusable generic tests and one-off singular tests.

scenes.title: How a dbt test works
bullets: A test is a query that returns failing rows
Zero rows returned means the test passes
Tests run as part of dbt build
scenes.narration: A dbt test is nothing more than a SQL query designed to return the rows that violate a rule. If the query returns no rows the test passes, and if it returns any rows the test fails and dbt reports exactly how many. Because tests run as part of dbt build, data quality is checked every time your pipeline executes.

scenes.title: Generic versus Singular tests
scenes.narration: Generic tests are reusable and parameterized, declared in YAML against a column and applied across many models. dbt ships four built-in generics: unique, not null, accepted values, and relationships, which checks referential integrity. Singular tests, by contrast, are hand-written SQL files in the tests directory that express one very specific business rule too bespoke to generalize.

scenes.title: Generic tests in YAML
scenes.code:
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'returned']
scenes.narration: Here we attach generic tests to a model's columns in YAML. The order_id column is asserted to be both unique and never null, which validates our primary key. The status column uses accepted_values to guarantee it only ever contains one of three allowed strings. Declaring these checks alongside the model keeps the contract for the data close to the data itself.

scenes.title: A singular test
scenes.code:
-- tests/assert_positive_order_total.sql
select
    order_id,
    total_amount
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
where total_amount < 0
scenes.narration: This singular test encodes a business rule that order totals must never be negative. It simply selects any offending rows, and because a passing test returns nothing, an empty result means the rule holds. When it does fail, the returned rows tell you precisely which orders broke the rule, which makes debugging fast.

scenes.text: Test every primary key with unique and not_null, and reach for singular tests only when a rule is too specific to reuse.
scenes.narration: A strong baseline is to test every primary key with unique and not null, then layer on singular tests only when a rule is too specific to be worth generalizing, giving you broad coverage without excessive maintenance.
